essays.stem: Explain how light travels along an optical fibre, and describe the layers of a fibre cable from the centre outwards.
essays.modelAnswer: At the centre is the core, a very thin strand of pure glass that carries the light. Round it is the cladding, also glass, about 125 µm across, made so that light bends less easily in it than in the core. When light in the core hits the boundary at a shallow angle, it is reflected back in. This is total internal reflection, and it keeps the light bouncing along the core for long distances, even round gentle bends. Over the cladding is a thin plastic coating that protects the glass from scratches and moisture, and in many cables a thicker buffer. Then come strength members, such as aramid yarn or a fibreglass rod, which take the pull when the cable is installed. The outer jacket protects everything from water, sunlight and damage; some outdoor cables also have armour.
markingPoints: Core carries the light
Cladding round the core; light reflects back at the boundary (total internal reflection)
Coating/buffer protects the glass
Strength members (aramid yarn or rod) take the pulling force
Outer jacket (and armour) protects against water, sun and damage

essays.stem: Compare singlemode and multimode fibre. Say how they differ and where each is best used.
essays.modelAnswer: Singlemode fibre has a very small core, about 9 µm, so the light travels in one path. It loses little light and the signal stays clean over long distances, so it is used for links of many kilometres, such as between towns, along roads and to homes for internet. It needs laser light sources, usually at 1310 nm or 1550 nm, which cost more, and its jacket is often yellow. Multimode fibre has a larger core, 50 µm or 62.5 µm, so light travels in many paths. These paths spread the signal out, which limits the distance to a few hundred metres for high speeds. It can use cheaper LED or low-cost laser sources, usually at 850 nm, and the equipment costs less. It is used inside buildings and campuses, such as between floors of an office in New Kingston. Its jacket is often orange or aqua.
markingPoints: Singlemode: small core (about 9 µm), one light path
Singlemode: long distances, laser sources at 1310/1550 nm
Multimode: larger core (50 or 62.5 µm), many paths
Multimode: shorter distances inside buildings, cheaper sources at about 850 nm
Usual jacket colours or cost difference mentioned

essays.stem: Describe the safety precautions to follow when working with optical fibre at the Centre.
essays.modelAnswer: Never look into the end of a fibre, a connector or a port, because it may carry infrared laser light that you cannot see and that can harm the eye. Make sure light sources are off or disconnected before inspecting an end, and use an inspection scope, not your eye. Fibre off-cuts are tiny, sharp glass splinters that can go into the skin or eyes and are hard to find. Wear safety glasses, work on a dark mat so the scraps can be seen, pick them up with tape or tweezers, and put them in a marked scrap container with a lid. Do not eat, drink or smoke at the work area, and wash your hands after work. Isopropyl alcohol catches fire easily, so keep it in a closed container away from flames and the splicer's arc, and use it with good ventilation. Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Never look into fibre ends; light sources off; use a scope
Glass splinters: safety glasses, dark mat, tape or tweezers
Scrap container with a lid
No eating, drinking or smoking; wash hands
Isopropyl alcohol: flammable, closed container, ventilation

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to prepare a fibre end ready for splicing.
essays.modelAnswer: First put on safety glasses and set out a dark work mat and a scrap container. Strip back the outer jacket to the length the splice tray or maker's guide gives, using a jacket stripper, without nicking the fibres. Cut the aramid yarn back with special shears. Remove the buffer tube or tight buffer with the right tool, then strip the thin coating from the glass in small sections with a precision fibre stripper, held at the right angle so the glass is not scratched. Clean the bare glass with a lint-free wipe and isopropyl alcohol, pulling it through once; after this do not touch the glass. Slide the splice protector onto one fibre if fusion splicing. Place the fibre in the cleaver at the length the maker gives and cleave it so the end is flat and square. Put the off-cut straight into the scrap container.
markingPoints: Sets up PPE, dark mat and scrap container
Strips jacket, cuts strength yarn and removes buffer correctly
Strips the coating with a precision stripper without damaging glass
Cleans with lint-free wipe and alcohol and does not touch the glass after
Cleaves at the correct length to a flat, square end; disposes of the off-cut

essays.stem: Compare fusion splicing and mechanical splicing. Describe how each joins the fibres and when each might be chosen.
essays.modelAnswer: In fusion splicing, the two cleaved fibre ends are placed in a fusion splicer. The machine lines them up using cameras, then melts them together with a small electric arc, so they become one piece of glass. The joint is then covered with a heat-shrink splice protector and stored in a splice tray. Fusion splices give the lowest loss and the least reflection and last a long time, but the splicer is expensive and needs power, care and training. In mechanical splicing, the two cleaved ends are pushed into a small sleeve that holds them in line, with a gel that matches the glass to reduce reflection. No arc or power is needed and the tools are cheap, but the loss is higher. Fusion is chosen for long links and many joints, such as in a telecom network. Mechanical splices suit quick repairs, few joints, or where no splicer is available.
markingPoints: Fusion: ends aligned and melted with an electric arc
Fusion: lowest loss, protected by heat-shrink sleeve, but costly equipment
Mechanical: ends held in an aligning sleeve with index-matching gel
Mechanical: cheap, no power, but higher loss
Sensible use for each (long/many joints vs quick repair/no splicer)

essays.stem: Explain why the end-face of a fibre connector must be clean, and describe how to inspect and clean it.
essays.modelAnswer: The core of a fibre is far thinner than a hair, so a speck of dust, oil from a finger or a drop of water on the end-face can block much of the light. This raises the loss of the link and causes reflections. When the connector is pushed into another, the dirt can also be pressed in and scratch or pit both end-faces for good. So the rule is: inspect before you connect. Make sure no light source is connected, then look at the end-face with a fibre inspection scope. If it is dirty, clean it with a dry lint-free cleaning tool or a one-click cleaner, or with a lint-free wipe and a little isopropyl alcohol followed by a dry wipe, as the maker says. Inspect it again. If it is still dirty or scratched, clean again or replace it. Keep dust caps on until the moment of connecting.
markingPoints: Dirt blocks light: high loss and reflections
Dirt can scratch or damage end-faces when mated
Inspect with a scope, with no light source connected
Clean with a proper dry cleaner or lint-free wipe and alcohol; inspect again
Keep dust caps on until connecting

essays.stem: Describe how to install a fibre cable in a duct or cable tray without damaging it.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the cable maker's data sheet for the largest pulling force and the minimum bend radius. Check the route and the duct for sharp edges and blockages. Fit a pulling grip to the strength members, not to the fibres or connectors, and use a swivel so the cable does not twist. Pull slowly and steadily, by hand or with a tension-limited winch, with one person feeding the cable at the start so it does not kink or rub. Use cable lubricant in long ducts if the maker allows. Do not bend the cable tighter than the minimum bend radius, especially at corners and pull boxes. In trays, lay the cable in neatly and hold it with hook-and-loop straps or loose ties, never crushed. Leave a service loop at each end for terminating and repairs. Label the cable at both ends and at access points.
markingPoints: Uses the maker's data for pulling force and bend radius
Pulls on the strength members with a grip and swivel
Pulls steadily with a feeder; avoids kinks
Keeps bends above the minimum radius; does not crush with ties
Leaves service loops and labels both ends

essays.stem: Explain how to measure the loss of a fibre link with a light source and an optical power meter, and how to work out the result.
essays.modelAnswer: First check that the light source and meter are set to the same wavelength, for example 850 nm for multimode or 1310 nm for singlemode, and let the source warm up. Clean and inspect all the test cords. Set a reference: connect the source to the meter with the test cord and record the reading, for example −20.0 dBm, or set the meter to zero on its reference setting. Then connect the source to one end of the link and the meter to the other end, using the test cords. Read the meter, for example −22.6 dBm. The loss is the difference between the reference and the reading: −20.0 − (−22.6) = 2.6 dB. Compare this with the loss expected from the design. Test each fibre and record the fibre number, the wavelength, the loss, the date and who tested it. Never look into the source or the ends while testing.
markingPoints: Same wavelength on source and meter; clean test cords
Sets a reference reading with the test cord
Connects source and meter at opposite ends and takes a reading
Loss = reference minus reading, worked correctly (2.6 dB in the example)
Compares with expected loss and records the results; eye safety

essays.stem: Describe how a visual fault locator is used to find faults in a fibre, and say what an OTDR can do that it cannot.
essays.modelAnswer: A visual fault locator is a small tester that sends bright red visible light into a fibre through its connector. It is used on short lengths, such as patch cords, links inside a building and splice trays. Where the fibre is broken, cracked or bent too tightly, the red light leaks out and the jacket or splice glows, so you can see where the fault is. It also shows that light gets to the far end, so it checks continuity and helps find which fibre is which. You look for the glow from the side, or let the light fall on a white card at the far end, and never look into the fibre end. An OTDR sends pulses of light down the fibre and measures the light that comes back. It shows a trace with the distance to each splice, connector and break, and their losses, even on links many kilometres long.
markingPoints: VFL sends visible red light into the fibre
Breaks, cracks and tight bends glow, showing where the fault is
Checks continuity / identifies fibres on short links
Look from the side or on a card, never into the end
OTDR gives the distance and loss of each event, over long links

essays.stem: A business in Kingston is choosing between copper data cable and fibre to link two buildings. Explain the advantages and disadvantages of fibre for this job.
essays.modelAnswer: Fibre has several advantages. It carries far more data than copper and over much longer distances, so the link will still be fast enough when the business grows. It uses light, not electricity, so it is not affected by electrical noise from motors or lightning, and it does not carry a voltage between the two buildings, which removes earth problems and lightning surges between them. It cannot easily be tapped, so it is more secure, and it is light and thin. There are some disadvantages. The equipment at each end costs more than copper equipment. Terminating and splicing need special tools, such as cleavers and splicers, and trained people. The glass can break if it is bent too tightly or crushed, so it must be installed with care. Fibre does not carry electrical power, so cameras or phones at the far end need their own supply.
markingPoints: More data over longer distances
Not affected by electrical noise; no voltage or lightning path between buildings
More secure, light and thin
Disadvantage: costlier end equipment and special tools/training
Disadvantage: fragile if bent or crushed, and carries no power

practical1.title: Strip, clean, cleave and join fibres, then check them with a fault locator
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a safe fibre work area with a dark mat and a scrap container. Each member prepares at least two fibre ends from a short length of loose-tube or tight-buffered cable: strip the jacket, cut the strength yarn, remove the buffer and coating, clean and cleave. Then join the ends. If the Centre has a fusion splicer, each member makes one fusion splice and fits a splice protector, under the assessor's watch. If there is no fusion splicer, each member makes one mechanical splice or fits one field-installable (mechanical) connector instead, following the maker's instructions. Place the finished joints in a splice tray. The assessor then connects a visual fault locator to one end, and the group checks each joint by looking at it from the side and seeing the red light on a white card at the far end. Never look into a fibre end. Record each joint and its result. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Short lengths of fibre optic cable (singlemode or multimode)
Jacket stripper, special shears for strength yarn, precision fibre stripper
Lint-free wipes and isopropyl alcohol in a closed dispenser
Fusion splicer and splice protectors, if the Centre has them; otherwise mechanical splices or field-installable connectors
Visual fault locator (used by the assessor), white card
Dark work mat, scrap container with lid, safety glasses
photos: The work area set up with mat, scrap container and PPE
A fibre end stripped and cleaned, ready to cleave
A finished splice (fusion with protector, or mechanical) or a fitted connector
The joints placed neatly in the splice tray
The red light seen on the card at the far end, and the results sheet
checklist: Wore safety glasses and kept the work area free of food and drink
Stripped the jacket, yarn and coating without damaging the glass
Cleaned the bare fibre and did not touch it afterwards
Cleaved at the correct length and put the off-cut in the scrap container
Made a splice or fitted a connector by the maker's method
Placed joints in the tray without tight bends
Never looked into a fibre end; checked the glow from the side or on the card
Recorded results and cleaned up the work area
safety: Never look into a fibre end or connector, even when you think no light is on it
Wear safety glasses; collect every glass off-cut with tape or tweezers into the closed scrap container
Isopropyl alcohol catches fire easily: keep it closed and away from heat and the splicer arc
No eating or drinking at the bench; wash your hands after the task

practical2.title: Install, label and test a short fibre link between two patch panels
practical2.brief: As a group, install a short fibre link (about 10–20 m) in the Centre's training bay, between two patch panels or wall boxes, using pre-terminated cable or cable terminated in Practical 1. Read the maker's data for bend radius and pulling force. Route the cable through the tray or duct, keeping bends gentle, hold it with hook-and-loop straps (not tight ties), and leave a service loop at each end. Label the cable and every port at both ends. Inspect and clean every connector before it is mated. The assessor then sets up the light source and power meter, and the group takes a reference reading, measures the loss of each fibre, works out the loss and records it with the date and tester's name. If the Centre has no power meter, check each fibre end to end with the visual fault locator instead, and write on the record that the loss was not measured. Each member does part of the routing, labels or cleans at least one connector, and takes or works out one reading. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Fibre optic cable (pre-terminated, or from Practical 1) with its data sheet
Two patch panels or wall boxes, and patch cords
Cable tray or duct, hook-and-loop straps
Label printer or labels and marker
Fibre inspection scope and connector cleaning tools
Light source and optical power meter with test cords (set up by the assessor); or a visual fault locator if there is no meter
photos: The cable route through the tray or duct, with gentle bends
The service loop and the cable fixed with hook-and-loop straps
The labels on the cable and ports at both ends
A connector end-face seen through the inspection scope
The reference reading on the power meter
A loss reading for one fibre (or the red light at the far end), and the completed results sheet
checklist: Read and followed the maker's bend radius and pulling limits
Routed and fixed the cable neatly without crushing or tight bends
Left a service loop and labelled both ends clearly
Inspected and cleaned a connector before mating
Took or worked out a loss reading correctly (or did the continuity check)
Recorded results with the fibre number, wavelength, date and name
Never looked into a fibre end or port
safety: Never look into fibre ends, ports or the light source; caps on unused ports
Use steps safely when working on high trays; keep three points of contact
Keep the floor clear of cable and tools while routing
Handle cleaning alcohol away from heat and keep it closed
